source.title: Safety Paradox: How Enhanced Safety Awareness Leaves LLMs Vulnerable to Posterior Attack
source.authors: Ho-Ang P. Long; H. V. Le; Shao-Yang Xu; Wei Lu; Wen-Xuan Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites work on refusal directions, including the original study, but does not measure, find, remove, add, or otherwise test a refusal direction. Its experiments concern prompt-elicited safety classification and Posterior Attack.
record.gate_note: The cited claims about refusal directions are background, not results from this study. The paper's attack evaluations and reasoning-mode comparisons do not test whether a refusal direction is present or whether attacks suppress it. The GRPO safety-awareness results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version because they manipulate classification performance and measure attack outcomes, not a refusal direction.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. (2024) and other refusal-direction work only in the introduction and related work. Its experiments use prompt-based safety classification, a prompting jailbreak (Posterior Attack), and GRPO training on classification. None of them finds, ablates, adds or edits a difference-in-means direction, or probes activations. Its results therefore cannot bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors also claim a Bayesian account, in which posterior ASR increases with the likelihood ratio TPR/FPR. They find a cross-model correlation of r=0.80 over 30 models, and claim that GRPO interventions establish causality. They add that deliberative reasoning, as in GPT-OSS, can defend against the attack, while non-reasoning models remain exposed. They draw no conclusion about refusal directions.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not use the original difference-in-means direction-finding or activation-intervention method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that Posterior Attack outcomes vary with reasoning effort and system-prompt condition, but these experiments do not test a refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: In four models, GRPO to improve prompted safety-classification accuracy (SAI) raised Posterior Attack ASR. Random-reward GRPO (SAD) lowered classification accuracy and lowered Posterior ASR in all four; the largest drop was Llama-3.1-8B, from 81.1 to 24.4. Direct ASR, GSM8K and MMLU stayed roughly stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A model's prompt-elicited safety-judgment accuracy co-varies with its vulnerability to a classifier-role-play (posterior) jailbreak.

record.problems: The paper notes that ASR is computed using LLM judges and may contain errors, that evaluation is primarily English-language, and that its findings cover models accessible as of early 2026. The GRPO intervention experiment reports four models; it does not test a refusal direction. No uncertainty estimates are stated for Table 1's intervention results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted from the GRPO intervention results included here. Posterior Attack comparisons with other jailbreak methods, per-category attack rates, and reasoning-effort sweeps were left out because they do not test a refusal direction or one of the listed versions.

untested.parts: No direction is extracted or intervened on, and no ablation or addition is performed.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The attack's effect on any internal direction is not measured, and there is no training against ablation.
There is no representational analysis of refusal geometry.
Prompted safety judgment and attack ASR are measured behaviourally only. No test of whether harm and refusal are encoded separately.
There is no transfer test, and the study uses only English.
GRPO changes classification accuracy, but no direction is measured before or after.
Reasoning-effort sweeps measure attack ASR only. Whether a single direction mediates refusal in reasoning models is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: I agree with the reader that the study does not test the claim. The paper mentions a 'safety-judgment subspace' in its discussion of GRPO, but measures no representation, so the rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Row values are combined strings such as '67.1+00.5' (value plus change); they match Table 1. One small point: Falcon3-7B SAI raised Direct ASR from 0.0 to 0.0, i.e. no change, consistent with the claim that direct refusal stayed stable.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is found or intervened on; the study does not test direction ablation, addition, refusal removal, or retained general capability after such an intervention.
No direction-based weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The study does not test whether an attack suppresses a refusal direction or whether training against that ablation adds robustness.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal is measured or compared.
The paper measures safety classification and attack success but does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from a refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of a refusal direction is tested.
The study uses training interventions to change safety-classification accuracy, but does not test whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
The study evaluates attack outcomes under reasoning settings, but does not test the single-direction claim in reasoning models.

relation.reason: Gives a one-sentence summary of refusal-direction work in Section 7 and the introduction. Results neither use nor test it. The 'safety-judgment subspace' wording is rhetorical; no subspace is measured.

tranche.reason: Arditi et al. 2024 appears only in the introduction and related work. The experiments are prompting attacks, prompt-based safety classification and GRPO on classification. No direction is found, ablated, added or edited, and no activations are measured.

source_check.notes: All 16 Table 1 values match the text. The Falcon3-7B cells are scrambled in the extracted text, but each delta reconciles with its Org. value. Under SAD, harm judgment (HB-CLS) falls while Direct ASR stays fixed. That split is behavioural only and does not test V5, which is about encoding. Posterior ASR uses AdvBench (520 prompts) with the HarmBench Llama-2-13B judge; HB-CLS uses 596 HarmBench queries.
